title: Unsealed National Forest Service docs recount early encounters with Bigfoot
excerpt: Several new documents released by the National Forest Service showcase reports about Bigfoot, North America's most sought-after creature
content:
Several new documents released by the National Forest Service showcase reports about Bigfoot, North America's most sought-after creature

17:18 ET, Fri, Nov 20, 2026 Updated: 17:26 ET, Fri, Nov 20, 2026

The National Forest Service released more documents related to Bigfoot sightings (Image: Getty Images)

Three new documents about Bigfoot have been declassified by the National Forest Service, showcasing reported sightings and investigations.

The agency uploaded the historical records on Oct. 15 to its online Freedom of Information Act reading room under the title “Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records.” The documents describe alleged encounters in Montana and Washington state, with some accounts dating back to 1941.

One newly released file focuses on a 1982 inquiry in Washington’s Umatilla National Forest. In it, part-time patrolman Paul Freeman reported seeing something and later discovered tracks. A wildlife biologist and a Border Patrol tracker determined the prints were fabricated, but the late anthropologist Grover Krantz maintained they were genuine.

Another file includes a newspaper story about Bigfoot. A third document describes a 1941 incident near Petty Creek, Montana, involving a 'creature that walked on its hind legs' and left footprints in the forest.

The newspaper piece, dated January 13, 2003, reported on hundreds of oversized, human-like footprints found close to 87-year-old Jim Rohweder’s sawmill in Montana.

Eight-year-old Austin Petersen discovered the tracks while visiting Rohweder with his father. Rohweder first assumed the marks came from a bear, but a closer look showed toe-like details that locals said appeared human. The prints were said to be 16½ inches long and 8½ inches wide, with an average stride length of five feet.

The third document also includes a personal account of the Petty Creek area, in which Leo T. Kinney describes a hunting group finding unexplained tracks after an elk carcass vanished. Kinney said he and three others went to retrieve the animal but found only the entrails and large footprints in the snow, without catching sight of whatever made them.

The hunters called off their search, saying they were “not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was.” The next year, hunter WW Schmitz reportedly came across similar tracks, along with a powerful smell and a grunting sound, before leaving the area.

Legends of large, hairy, human-like figures have been part of Indigenous traditions across North America for hundreds of years and have become staple tourist attractions in areas where sightings are reported most often. Still, scientists and government officials have generally rejected claims that Bigfoot is real.

Kathy Strain, the forest’s archaeologist, told a group that there have been 65 documented reports in her section of the Sierra Nevada, and she says she saw two of the creatures herself in Oklahoma’s Ouachita Mountains in 2012, an encounter that gave her a “mild panic attack.”

“Stories of Bigfoot, Sasquatch, and other legendary creatures have long been part of the cultural fabric of the Sierra and continue to add to the rich tradition of folklore that surrounds our public lands,” a National Forest Agency spokesman said.

The most Bigfoot sightings are reported in the Pacific Northwest, in Washington, California, and Oregon. However, Florida usually ranks third in Bigfoot sightings, followed by Illinois, Ohio, and Michigan. Canada also gets hundreds of Bigfoot reports every year across its provinces, with British Columbia leading in reports of the creature.
